item.title: How big donors influence my decisions as a small donor
item.description:
Published on November 23, 2026 9:37 PM GMT

The biggest donors in AI safety have (in my view) certain biases that cause them to disregard important cause areas. This fact informs my cause prioritization.

I don't usually think about it directly. However:

  • I have certain ideas about what interventions are most cost-effective at the margin: namely, AI pause advocacy; especially public advocacy; especially especially loud, visible advocacy like protests.
  • A big driver of that cost-effectiveness is neglectedness. If there were as much money in AI pause advocacy as there is in prosaic alignment research, I wouldn't favor it as much.
  • This kind of advocacy is neglected; almost all big funders dislike this kind of advocacy; that's not a coincidence.

Big donors' decisions indirectly play into my prioritization because they affect which causes are most neglected. You can see this in my choice to donate to AI pause advocacy, and in the fact that I put high priority on neglected aspects of sentient welfare (even though I don't fund them).

It's also worth considering how future donations from Anthropic equity holders might come into play, which I will do near the end of this post.

Cross-posted from my website.

How neglectedness matters

My favorite cause areas tend to be highly neglected. The basic reason to care about neglectedness is that interventions have diminishing marginal utility of spending; the first dollars matter the most. But sometimes a cause is neglected because it's bad. Why is nobody spending money trying to convert all the matter in the universe into paperclips? It's highly neglected! But also, it's a really bad idea, and nobody should spend money on it.

If a cause is neglected, it's nice to have some explanation of why it's neglected. If it's so good, why is nobody doing it? If I can point to some bias that causes other donors to overlook it, then that increases my confidence that the cause area isn't neglected simply because it's bad.

Big donors and AI pause advocacy

Why do big funders dislike AI pause advocacy? If they have good reasons that I'm not aware of, then that's an argument against donating to it. But: (1) insofar as they have articulated their reasons, I disagree with them; (2) there are visible biases that push away from loud AI risk advocacy.

The establishment wing of the AI safety field, which includes most of the big funders, has historically put too much emphasis on respectability. Funding disproportionately went to those with the most mainstream prestige,[1] and continues to disproportionately focus on inside-game tactics. There is this idea that you can't talk publicly about extinction risk, that you have to downplay your concerns so that you sound sane. I considered this plausible for a long time, but in retrospect I think it has made things worse by ceding a lot of power to AI companies and delaying public awareness of the risks.

I remember reading Let's think about slowing down AI in 2022, and thinking, how is it that someone is just now writing this post in 2022? It could've been written years ago, but it wasn't.

The biggest actors in AI safety have major conflicts of interest. They stand to make a lot of money off of AI, and they have a lot of friends working on AI. Pausing AI would cause them to lose money and could damage their personal relationships.

(This is especially true if you count AI companies themselves as the biggest actors in AI safety, which in some sense they are.)

When Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) gave $30 million to OpenAI in 2017, the grant writeup said:

Relationship disclosures

OpenAI researchers Dario Amodei and Paul Christiano are both technical advisors to Open Philanthropy and live in the same house as Holden. In addition, Holden is engaged to Dario’s sister Daniela.

Some people raised concerns about this. At the time, I thought it was a bad idea to give money to OpenAI, but I also believed the grantmakers were trustworthy and minimally biased; we just had some disagreements about the merits of this grant. But having seen how things have evolved since then, I'm much more willing to believe that conflicts of interest played an important role.

Big donors and sentient welfare

For the last three years, I've exclusively donated to AI pause advocacy. However, I still believe sentient welfare is a strong candidate for the best place to donate.

Effective altruism is about going beyond your personal biases to do what's most effective. But the EA community—including, but not limited to, the big foundations—still falls too much into some standard biases. Three important ones are:

  1. Caring more about human-caused suffering than suffering from other sources.
  2. Caring more about beings that look and act sympathetic.
  3. Caring more about presently-occurring suffering than future suffering.

The first bias causes people—even people who care about animal welfare—to neglect wild animal suffering. Unlike farm animals, wild animals mostly do not suffer as a result of human activity. Some people see farm animal suffering as worse because it's "our fault"; in my view, suffering is suffering.[2] Of course wild animal suffering is difficult to do anything about, but that is not sufficient to explain why it gets so little funding.

The second bias causes people to pay much more attention to mammals and birds than to fish or, especially, invertebrates. Shrimp welfare has gotten more interest recently with the Shrimp Welfare Project getting some publicity and earning a recommendation from Animal Charity Evaluators starting in 2023, but (1) shrimp welfare still gets far less funding than farmed mammal welfare, and (2) non-shrimp invertebrates remain even more neglected. If I made a list of everyone who's done serious work on soil invertebrate welfare, it would be shorter than my last grocery list.[3]

(In 2016, I argued that Coefficient Giving should put higher priority on wild animal suffering, especially because their position as a grantmaker makes them unusually well-suited to tackle the tractability problem. They've given it more than zero funding since then, but not much more.)

The neglect of "weird" cause areas like invertebrate welfare, even among people who specifically focus on neglected causes, is all the more reason why small donors like me should pay attention to those causes. I haven't donated to them recently—I prefer AI pause advocacy—but they're still high on my priorities list, and that's partly because other donors avoid them.[4]

Future Anthropic donors

Many Anthropic employees intend to donate a lot of money; there has been much discussion of how to respond to this incoming wave of funding. I have cautioned against taking the money for granted; there are a lot of reasons why this wave of funding might fail to materialize, or why it might be much smaller than you'd think. That aside, how does this potential influx of donations affect my own donations today?

My primary thought is that I can't reliably predict where that money will go or when, so it shouldn't influence my decisions too much.

My secondary thought is that this future funding weakly supports my decision to prioritize AI pause advocacy. Anthropic donors are the sorts of people who decided to work at Anthropic. If I work at Anthropic, then presumably I think it's a better idea to keep doing that than to loudly quit and do public advocacy instead, like Jacob Coxon and Daniel Kokotajlo did. If that's what I believe, then I'm probably also less likely to fund public advocacy.

What's more, if my job and most of my net worth are tied up with Anthropic's valuation, then I'm less likely to support something that might hurt Anthropic. Pausing AI would indirectly hurt me.

(I'm sure there are plenty of individual Anthropic employees who would support AI pause advocacy—I know there are more than zero—but as a whole, they will be biased against it.)

Regarding sentient welfare, the situation appears to be reversed: Anthropic employees are unusually likely to care about weird things like invertebrate welfare and digital sentience. I'm cautiously optimistic that those areas will see increased funding in the near future.

Future Anthropic funding is too uncertain to weigh heavily. But insofar as Anthropic money influences my donations, it's an additional reason for me to give to AI pause advocacy rather than sentient welfare.

Header image credit: Glen Carrie

  1. In the most relevant passage (the four paragraphs starting from "The same year that OpenAI launched..."), Richard Ngo argues that Holden Karnofsky initially disregarded MIRI's AI risk arguments largely because MIRI was not a prestigious source. Later, when he became convinced that AI risk was a big deal, most Coefficient Giving money went to orgs with legible prestige; "this led MIRI to become a small, niche part of the field that it had founded." ↩︎

  2. It is difficult to justify caring about farm animals over wild animals, even given a view where you ought to care more about suffering that you are personally responsible for. When I donate to farm animal advocacy, I'm not helping animals that I personally would have harmed otherwise. I'm helping animals that other people would have harmed.

    On an emotional level, people care more about intentional harms—a murder is more likely to make the news than a death by heart attack. Part of why EAs fund global health interventions is that global health is boring; malaria doesn't catch headlines, so EAs find low-hanging fruit there. Wild animal welfare is boring in the same way. Factory farming is somebody's fault; wild animal suffering is just kinda there. ↩︎

  3. I'm talking about a particularly neglected subset of animal welfare, but even animal welfare as a whole is neglected among cause-neutral donors. Ariel Simnegar wrote Open Phil [a.k.a. Coefficient Giving] Should Allocate Most Neartermist Funding to Animal Welfare. There are strong arguments that animal welfare ought to receive more EA funding than global poverty, but much more money goes to global poverty—both Coefficient Giving money, and EA money more broadly. ↩︎

  4. I say "partly" because neglectedness is not the only reason to prioritize them. For example, wild animal welfare is a vastly larger problem than farm animal welfare. Even if it received 10x as much funding, wild animal welfare might still be the better place for marginal donations to go. ↩︎

But sometimes a cause is neglected because it's bad. Why is nobody spending money trying to convert all the matter in the universe into paperclips? It's highly neglected! But also, it's a really bad idea, and nobody should spend money on it.

If a cause is neglected, it's nice to have some explanation of why it's neglected. If it's so good, why is nobody doing it? If I can point to some bias that causes other donors to overlook it, then that increases my confidence that the cause area isn't neglected simply because it's bad.

Big donors and AI pause advocacy

Why do big funders dislike AI pause advocacy? If they have good reasons that I'm not aware of, then that's an argument against donating to it. But: (1) insofar as they have articulated their reasons, I disagree with them; (2) there are visible biases that push away from loud AI risk advocacy.

The establishment wing of the AI safety field, which includes most of the big funders, has historically put too much emphasis on respectability. Funding disproportionately went to those with the most mainstream prestige,[1] and continues to disproportionately focus on inside-game tactics. There is this idea that you can't talk publicly about extinction risk, that you have to downplay your concerns so that you sound sane. I considered this plausible for a long time, but in retrospect I think it has made things worse by ceding a lot of power to AI companies and delaying public awareness of the risks.

I remember reading Let's think about slowing down AI in 2022, and thinking, how is it that someone is just now writing this post in 2022? It could've been written years ago, but it wasn't.

The biggest actors in AI safety have major conflicts of interest. They stand to make a lot of money off of AI, and they have a lot of friends working on AI. Pausing AI would cause them to lose money and could damage their personal relationships.

(This is especially true if you count AI companies themselves as the biggest actors in AI safety, which in some sense they are.)

When Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) gave $30 million to OpenAI in 2017, the grant writeup said:

Relationship disclosures

OpenAI researchers Dario Amodei and Paul Christiano are both technical advisors to Open Philanthropy and live in the same house as Holden. In addition, Holden is engaged to Dario’s sister Daniela.

Some people raised concerns about this. At the time, I thought it was a bad idea to give money to OpenAI, but I also believed the grantmakers were trustworthy and minimally biased; we just had some disagreements about the merits of this grant. But having seen how things have evolved since then, I'm much more willing to believe that conflicts of interest played an important role.

Big donors and sentient welfare

For the last three years, I've exclusively donated to AI pause advocacy. However, I still believe sentient welfare is a strong candidate for the best place to donate.

Effective altruism is about going beyond your personal biases to do what's most effective. But the EA community—including, but not limited to, the big foundations—still falls too much into some standard biases. Three important ones are:

  1. Caring more about human-caused suffering than suffering from other sources.
  2. Caring more about beings that look and act sympathetic.
  3. Caring more about presently-occurring suffering than future suffering.

The first bias causes people—even people who care about animal welfare—to neglect wild animal suffering. Unlike farm animals, wild animals mostly do not suffer as a result of human activity. Some people see farm animal suffering as worse because it's "our fault"; in my view, suffering is suffering.[2] Of course wild animal suffering is difficult to do anything about, but that is not sufficient to explain why it gets so little funding.

The second bias causes people to pay much more attention to mammals and birds than to fish or, especially, invertebrates. Shrimp welfare has gotten more interest recently with the Shrimp Welfare Project getting some publicity and earning a recommendation from Animal Charity Evaluators starting in 2023, but (1) shrimp welfare still gets far less funding than farmed mammal welfare, and (2) non-shrimp invertebrates remain even more neglected. If I made a list of everyone who's done serious work on soil invertebrate welfare, it would be shorter than my last grocery list.[3]

(In 2016, I argued that Coefficient Giving should put higher priority on wild animal suffering, especially because their position as a grantmaker makes them unusually well-suited to tackle the tractability problem. They've given it more than zero funding since then, but not much more.)

The neglect of "weird" cause areas like invertebrate welfare, even among people who specifically focus on neglected causes, is all the more reason why small donors like me should pay attention to those causes. I haven't donated to them recently—I prefer AI pause advocacy—but they're still high on my priorities list, and that's partly because other donors avoid them.[4]

Future Anthropic donors

Many Anthropic employees intend to donate a lot of money; there has been much discussion of how to respond to this incoming wave of funding. I have cautioned against taking the money for granted; there are a lot of reasons why this wave of funding might fail to materialize, or why it might be much smaller than you'd think. That aside, how does this potential influx of donations affect my own donations today?

My primary thought is that I can't reliably predict where that money will go or when, so it shouldn't influence my decisions too much.

My secondary thought is that this future funding weakly supports my decision to prioritize AI pause advocacy. Anthropic donors are the sorts of people who decided to work at Anthropic. If I work at Anthropic, then presumably I think it's a better idea to keep doing that than to loudly quit and do public advocacy instead, like Jacob Coxon and Daniel Kokotajlo did. If that's what I believe, then I'm probably also less likely to fund public advocacy.

What's more, if my job and most of my net worth are tied up with Anthropic's valuation, then I'm less likely to support something that might hurt Anthropic. Pausing AI would indirectly hurt me.

(I'm sure there are plenty of individual Anthropic employees who would support AI pause advocacy—I know there are more than zero—but as a whole, they will be biased against it.)

Regarding sentient welfare, the situation appears to be reversed: Anthropic employees are unusually likely to care about weird things like invertebrate welfare and digital sentience. I'm cautiously optimistic that those areas will see increased funding in the near future.

Future Anthropic funding is too uncertain to weigh heavily. But insofar as Anthropic money influences my donations, it's an additional reason for me to give to AI pause advocacy rather than sentient welfare.

Header image credit: Glen Carrie

item.title: Animal Welfare Fund: 2026 Breakthroughs for animals, and what we want to see in 2027
item.description:
Published on November 24, 2026 10:16 PM GMT

  • The EA Animal Welfare Fund saw several breakthroughs for animals in 2026 and for our fund itself. We set out to deploy $20M and we passed it, making more than 80 grants that align with our strategy, that cleared our bar for expected impact for dollar.
  • There are three moments this year that cleared our bar as a breakthrough: Asia, Latin America, and Africa now lead the world in new cage-free commitments; the European Commission committed to propose ending cages for laying hens; and Kenya became the first African country to adopt a national fish welfare standard.
  • Looking ahead to 2027, we have identified 100 opportunities we would like to fund, all directed toward more breakthrough moments we want to see for animals.

Three breakthroughs from 2026

We try not to use the word breakthrough lightly. For us, a breakthrough is a change that is likely to hold, opens up the door to major impact for animals, and gives advocates a playbook they can reuse and scale. We saw many incredible wins this year, thanks to our grantees and the wider movement. There are too many to list, so we picked three moments to highlight: 

Breakthrough 1: Asia, Latin America, and Africa now lead on new cage-free commitments

For years, cage-free progress happened mostly in the US and Europe, even though about 84% of the world's hens are farmed in Asia, Latin America, and Africa. That is changing. In 2026, 87% of all new cage-free pledges were secured in these three regions. A good measure of credit goes to the 80+ member groups of the Open Wing Alliance, who now campaign across 72 countries. This year we were able to support more of them in more places than ever before.

2025 was the largest deadline year so far for companies making pledges, with more than 1,000 pledges coming due worldwide, and another 200+ in 2026. There are good results in Latin America. The region has more than 300 pledges reported as fully implemented, more than any region except Europe and well ahead of North America. While the number of pledges doesn’t necessarily indicate a number of animals helped, we nevertheless see this as an exciting sign of gaining more momentum.

Efforts in Brazil to turn pledges into transitions

Brazil is the world's fifth-largest egg producer, and 2025 was the deadline for many of the nearly 190 companies there with cage-free pledges. Our grantee Fórum Nacional de Proteção e Defesa Animal (Fórum Animal), which we have funded since 2021, combined public pressure with transition support. They built Brazil's most comprehensive public record of which companies report cage-free progress, and with others launched a "Stop Humane Washing" campaign against companies that market welfare claims without changing practice.

Fórum Animal reported 90 of about 200 committed companies had reported progress, up from 69 a year earlier. They also shared that the companies it worked with now report progress covering about 9.9 million hens a year. They are part of the coalition holding these companies to their pledges, which together could help about 34.2 million hens a year.

Brazil is not alone. AWF grantees in several countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America are working with governments on national cage-free standards and labeling laws, work that could reach up to 27 million hens a year.

Breakthrough 2: the EU committed to propose to end cages

In July, the European Commission's Livestock Strategy committed to propose phasing out cages for laying hens by the end of 2026, alongside an end to the routine killing of day-old male chicks. More than 140 million hens in the EU are still caged, and the regulation would cover all 27 member states.

This has been a long time coming. The Commission first promised to end cages in 2021, after a European Citizens' Initiative gathered 1.4 million signatures, and it delayed the proposal repeatedly. Many groups kept up the pressure. We have funded national campaigns that we think helped build the case for the July proposal.

While this may be a breakthrough for hens and male chicks in Europe, it was also a breakthrough in how our fund works. For years our grant-making budget meant funding Europe one country at a time. This year, when the window opened, grantees we had backed for years were ready to move, and we funded a new coalition within seven days to coordinate pressure in Brussels and in every member state, and funded work in multiple countries at once.

What has happened since. In August, we opened a request for proposals for EU cage-free work, focused on lobbying for the strongest possible proposal and building support for it in the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. We set one goal across all grantees: a proposal with the shortest possible transition period, no open-ended exemptions, coverage for imported products, and finance to help farmers through the transition.

The proposal is not law yet. In early November, advocacy groups welcomed leaked plans to ban cages while criticizing a proposed 12-year transition. We agree that 12 years is too long. Once the Commission publishes its proposal, it must pass the European Parliament and the member states, and we expect this work to continue through 2027.

Breakthrough 3: Africa's first national fish welfare standard

Kenya became the first country in Africa to adopt a national fish welfare standard, and the government credits AWF grantee, One Health and Development Initiative (OHDI), with helping to develop it. We were encouraged to see this standard covers a fish’s whole life, starting in the hatchery. OHDI’s approach was to set up the framework, convene farmers, regulators, and other stakeholders, and build the tools to enforce the standard. It is using that approach in other countries across the continent. In Kenya and one other country where they are working, we think these standards could reach 300 to 500 million fish a year, about as many as all egg-laying hens farmed in the U.S. If all the countries where OHDI works adopt standards, that could rise to 1 billion to 3.8 billion fish a year. At the top of that range, that is more than all the pigs, cattle, and sheep slaughtered worldwide in a year combined.

What this shows us: Kenya shows that a national animal welfare standard can be won in Africa, and it raised our confidence in this route to change. We have started funding more policy work across the continent, for fish and for other farmed animals.

Where we invested in 2026

A year ago, I wrote about AWF's strategy and plans. We said we hoped to deploy $20 million in 2026. It seemed ambitious. Thanks to your donations and the work of our grantees, we have already exceeded that goal. As of November 10, we had approved or paid out 84 grants to scale or seed promising interventions for animals.

Here's where we scaled this year, with grants clearing our bar for expected impact per dollar.

Breakthroughs we want to see in 2027

For 2027, we have identified roughly 100 specific opportunities that we would like to fund. These are the breakthroughs we most want our 2027 grantmaking budget to achieve (shared in no particular sequence).

Ending cages for hens, including where most hens live

We plan to put about 30% of our 2027 portfolio into ending cages for laying hens. About 84% of the world's roughly 8 billion farmed hens are in Asia, Latin America, and Africa, where work needs to happen on the demand and supply level. So alongside corporate campaigns and accountability, we will fund producer training, links between buyers and compliant farms, national standards, and labeling laws. In Europe, we will back the push to turn the Commission's proposal into strong law.

Better lives for shrimp

About 440 billion shrimp are killed on farms each year, most of them inhumanely. Much of the work so far has focused on humane stunning at slaughter, including testing whether stunning works as intended, and on early on-farm trials. Next, we want to improve the whole of a shrimp's life. That means building the research base on what good welfare looks like on a farm, and piloting new welfare standards on farms.

Whole-life welfare standards for fish, written into law

What OHDI did in Kenya showed what is possible, and we want to scale these types of interventions, especially those that cover a fish’s whole life. We will also fund on-farm pilots and local university research so that new standards rest on evidence that holds up in a regional context. In Africa alone, this work could eventually cover 1 billion to 3.8 billion fish a year.

Practical interventions for wild animals

In 2027, we want to shorten the time between research on wild animal welfare and interventions that help animals, prioritizing those that are evidence-based, tractable and low-risk.

A movement big enough to do all of this

None of the breakthroughs above happen without skilled advocates and strong organizations, and right now that capacity is one of the movement's biggest bottlenecks. Our grants for movement-wide work increased significantly in 2026. We funded the training and incubation of new campaign groups, helped advocates connect, increased their capacity to help animals, funded forums to increase coordination of their efforts, and addressed the movement’s biggest monitoring, evaluation, and learning needs.

In 2027, we have much more to do: we could seed new charities through incubation, build talent pipelines, fund impact measurement, and help advocates plan for scale and keep impact as they grow. If the movement can double in size or more, our breakthroughs for animals become more reachable.

Thank you

None of this year's breakthroughs came from a single grant. Each followed years of funding to incredible groups that kept building on promising work. What made them possible was the work of inspiring advocates, and steady support from hundreds of monthly donors, many one-time gifts, and larger gifts to our pooled fund. A large, recurring pool of funding is what builds robustness and lets us commit to grantees for several years at once, so they can hire and take on bigger targets with confidence.

If you want to help make 2027's breakthroughs happen:

  • Give to the EA Animal Welfare Fund.
  • Talk with us about a multi-year or larger gift. Unrestricted gifts let us direct money where it can do the most good, and we are open to discussing restricted gifts too. Email me at karolina@effectivealtruismfunds.org.
